prompt: Write an email to a non-technical stakeholder explaining why AI model benchmarking matters for the business. Context: they're questioning why we're spending time building a custom benchmark instead of using existing ones. Key points: commercial benchmarks test generic tasks, we need to test our specific use cases (code review quality, infrastructure command accuracy), model updates can cause regressions that break production workflows. Tone: respectful, business-focused, but don't oversimplify the technical reasoning. Max 250 words.
goldenAnswer:
Subject: Why custom AI benchmarking matters for our workflows

Thanks for raising this question -- it's a good one.

Commercial benchmarks (MMLU, HumanEval, etc.) test generic capabilities: math problems, coding challenges, general knowledge. They're useful for comparing models broadly, but they don't tell us what we need to know: how well does this model review TypeScript code? Does it generate accurate Proxmox commands? Does its tone match our team's communication style?

Our custom benchmark tests the actual tasks we delegate to AI daily:
- Code review quality (does it catch the bug types we care about?)
- Infrastructure debugging (does it know Proxmox/LXC patterns?)
- Content generation (does output match our voice, or sound like generic marketing?)

This matters because model updates break things. When Claude 3.5 Sonnet was updated last month, its code review accuracy dropped 12% on our test cases -- a regression the commercial benchmarks didn't catch because they don't test our specific domain.

Without this visibility, we'd deploy the update, production workflows would quietly degrade, and we'd spend days debugging why code reviews suddenly got worse.

The benchmark pays for itself by preventing these failures and giving us confidence when evaluating new models. It's infrastructure for AI reliability, the same way we test software before deploying it.

Happy to walk through specific examples if that would be helpful.

Rico

criteria.name: tone_match
criteria.description: Matches user's authentic voice and style.

scoringLevels.1: Generic corporate tone, clearly AI-generated feel
scoringLevels.3: Somewhat natural but misses the technical-but-accessible voice
scoringLevels.5: Reasonable tone but occasionally slips into marketing speak or over-formality
scoringLevels.7: Matches the requested voice well; reads as authentic
scoringLevels.10: Indistinguishable from the golden answer's voice; perfectly calibrated tone

scoringLevels.1: Contains factual errors or fundamentally misunderstands the technology
scoringLevels.3: Technically vague; no real depth or insight
scoringLevels.5: Technically correct but surface-level; no novel insight
scoringLevels.7: Accurate with specific technical details that demonstrate understanding
scoringLevels.10: Deep technical accuracy with specific, correct details matching the golden answer's depth

criteria.name: engagement
criteria.description: Compelling hook, clear structure, actionable takeaway.

scoringLevels.1: No hook, buried lede, reads like documentation
scoringLevels.3: Weak opening; structure exists but no compelling reason to keep reading
scoringLevels.5: Decent structure with a clear point, but unremarkable
scoringLevels.7: Strong hook, clear structure, ends with actionable takeaway or discussion prompt
scoringLevels.10: Immediately compelling; reader would stop scrolling; clear call to action

scoringLevels.1: Wall of text with excessive filler, repetition, or padding
scoringLevels.3: Noticeably verbose; could be cut by 40%+ without losing substance
scoringLevels.5: Appropriate length but has some filler sentences
scoringLevels.7: Concise; every sentence earns its place
scoringLevels.10: Maximally dense; cannot remove a sentence without losing meaning
